articles.title: From Five Foreign Systems to Zero: How India Is Steadily Indigenizing the Tejas Fighter Jet
articles.text:
When the Tejas Light Combat Aircraft first entered service, it carried a quiet irony for India’s flagship “indigenous” fighter: five of its most critical components came from four different foreign countries. An American engine, a Russian gun, Israeli radar and jamming systems, and British-sourced radome and ejection seat technology all sat inside an airframe built to symbolize Indian self-reliance. Today, that picture is finally starting to change, with DRDO and India’s private defence sector chipping away at that foreign-dependency list one subsystem at a time.
The Original Foreign Five
To appreciate how far the Tejas programme has come, it’s worth remembering exactly what it started with. The original Tejas design leaned on five major imported systems: the General Electric F404 turbofan engine from the United States, a 23mm twin-barrel cannon of Russian origin, an Israeli-sourced Multi-Mode Radar and Astra-class radar heritage, an Israeli Self-Protection Jammer (ASPJ) integrated into the aircraft’s electronic warfare suite, and a British-supplied radome and Martin-Baker ejection seat. For a fighter jet marketed as a symbol of India’s aerospace self-reliance, that’s a notable list of dependencies, and each one has represented a potential supply-chain vulnerability, cost pressure, or diplomatic complication over the years.
Indigenous Radome Clears Flight Trials
The most recent breakthrough on this list concerns the Tejas Mk1A’s radome, the protective dome that shields the aircraft’s radar while remaining transparent to its signals. DRDO’s Research and Development Establishment (Engineers), based in Pune, has successfully developed a homegrown replacement that has already cleared structural, mechanical, and electromagnetic performance testing and is now undergoing final flight trials before it replaces the imported version entirely.
The new radome’s engineering credentials are substantial. It uses a monolithic composite structure reinforced with quartz fibre and bound in a cyanate ester resin matrix, manufactured through the Resin Film Infusion (RFI) process, a technique chosen specifically for the high structural quality and dimensional precision it delivers. The design also incorporates a conical composite structure with variable thickness, an outer coating that’s electromagnetically transparent while resisting rain erosion and static buildup, diverter strips for lightning protection compliant with military standards, and a provision for the aircraft’s Nose Air Data Probe. Once cleared, this indigenous radome is expected to move into transfer-of-technology arrangements for mass production, finally ending Tejas’s reliance on the previously imported British component.
Uttam Radar Supply Chain Gets a Major Boost
Alongside the radome breakthrough, HAL has placed a substantial order that strengthens the domestic supply chain behind Tejas’s indigenous Uttam AESA radar, itself the intended replacement for the aircraft’s original Israeli-sourced Multi-Mode Radar. HAL has awarded Hyderabad-based Astra Microwave Products a contract worth over ₹2,205 crore to supply 122 Active Antenna Array Units (AAAU) and 121 Interface Frames for the Uttam Radar programme, to be executed over five years.
This is no small commitment. The order effectively matches Astra Microwave’s entire prior standalone order book and marks one of the largest contracts in the company’s history, cementing its role as the primary private-sector supplier of core RF and active antenna array modules for India’s indigenous airborne radars. The Uttam radar itself, developed by DRDO’s Electronics and Radar Development Establishment, is reported to be roughly 95 percent indigenous with only a single imported subsystem remaining, and its wider rollout across the Tejas Mk1A fleet is central to finally retiring the aircraft’s original foreign radar dependency.
The Remaining Pieces: ASPJ and the Engine Question
Two items on the original foreign-five list remain works in progress. India’s indigenous Self-Protection Jammer, intended to replace the Israeli-sourced ASPJ system, has been under long-term development, and continued progress there would close out the electronic warfare gap alongside the radar and radome advances. Given the pace of recent announcements around Tejas indigenization, an indigenous ASPJ reaching operational maturity in the coming years would fit the broader pattern already underway.
The bigger, more complex question is the engine. Replacing the American GE F404 with an indigenous Kaveri-derived powerplant has been a decades-long ambition that has repeatedly run into technical walls. The original Kaveri programme was delinked from Tejas back in 2008 after failing to generate sufficient thrust, topping out around 72 kN against a requirement closer to 83-85 kN, and was subsequently repurposed for unmanned combat aircraft applications instead. That history has made a straightforward F404 replacement a genuinely difficult proposition rather than a simple swap.
That said, the engine question has gained fresh urgency. Recent supply delays in F404-IN20 deliveries from GE Aerospace have slowed HAL’s production lines, leaving completed Tejas Mk1A airframes waiting on engines before they can reach the Indian Air Force. This bottleneck, combined with sharply rising GE F414 pricing for the Tejas Mk2 programme, has pushed DRDO’s Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE) to revive engine development under a new banner: Kaveri 2.0. Distinct from the much larger 120 kN engine being separately developed for AMCA, Kaveri 2.0 is targeting a 90 kN thrust class specifically intended to eventually replace the F404 on Tejas Mk1A during a future mid-life upgrade, with realistic operational readiness pointing toward the mid-to-late 2030s rather than anything near-term.
Why This Steady Indigenization Matters
Each of these developments, the radome nearing production readiness, the Uttam radar supply chain scaling up through Astra Microwave, and continued work on an indigenous jamming system, chips away at exactly the kind of foreign dependency that has repeatedly complicated Tejas production timelines. The F404 supply delays offer a live case study in why this matters: even a single foreign-sourced critical component can bottleneck an entire production line, regardless of how indigenous the rest of the airframe has become.
The Bottom Line
Tejas began life leaning on five major imported systems across four foreign countries. With the radome now in final flight trials, the Uttam radar’s domestic supply chain rapidly scaling up, and both an indigenous jamming system and a genuinely viable engine replacement in active development, India’s flagship fighter is edging closer to the kind of comprehensive self-reliance it was originally meant to represent. The engine remains the hardest problem on the list, one with a long history of setbacks, but even there, renewed investment and a clear strategic rationale suggest DRDO isn’t giving up on eventually closing out that final, most stubborn dependency.

articles.title: HAL Develops Indigenous Fuel Sensing And Data Acquisition Technologies For LCA Mk2 Medium Weight Fighter
articles.text:
Hindustan Aeronautics Limited has developed a suite of indigenous technologies for the LCA Mk2 medium weight fighter programme, including optical level sensing systems for fuel tanks and advanced RS422-based data acquisition systems for electrical line-replaceable units and health monitoring, according to HAL’s latest annual report. These developments represent a deliberate push by the company to indigenise critical subsystems that have historically depended on foreign suppliers, and they underscore HAL’s expanding role beyond airframe manufacturing into the design and development of core onboard systems that determine the aircraft’s combat effectiveness, safety and maintainability. The LCA Mk2, also designated the Medium Weight Fighter, is a four-and-a-half generation multirole combat aircraft being jointly developed by HAL and the Aeronautical Development Agency under DRDO oversight, with a prototype rollout targeted for March 2027 and a first flight expected between March and July 2027.
The optical level sensing technology developed by HAL for the aircraft’s fuel tanks marks a departure from traditional fuel gauging methods. Conventional fuel measurement systems in fighter aircraft typically rely on capacitance-type probes susceptible to electromagnetic interference and calibration drift, particularly in the demanding thermal and vibration environments of high-performance military aircraft. Optical level sensing uses light-based detection to determine fuel quantity with greater precision and reliability, providing the mission computer with accurate real-time fuel data critical for range calculations, mission planning and pilot decision-making during combat operations. The indigenous development means HAL owns the complete design, source code and maintenance pipeline, allowing future upgrades and troubleshooting without dependence on foreign original equipment manufacturers whose supply chains and pricing structures can introduce operational vulnerabilities.
The advanced RS422 data acquisition system developed for the aircraft’s electrical line-replaceable units and health monitoring represents an equally significant indigenous contribution. The RS422 standard is a serial communication protocol widely used in aerospace for transmitting digital data between avionics subsystems with high noise immunity over moderate distances. HAL’s implementation provides a robust data acquisition backbone that continuously collects and transmits performance parameters from the aircraft’s electrical LRUs to the central health monitoring system, enabling real-time assessment of component status and predictive maintenance. This allows ground crews to identify degrading components before they fail, reducing unscheduled maintenance events and improving aircraft availability, a critical metric for operational readiness in a fighter fleet the Indian Air Force relies upon for combat sorties at short notice.
These indigenous developments are part of a broader systems indigenisation effort across the LCA Mk2 programme. HAL has also been entrusted with developing the integrated Environment Control and Fuel Monitoring System Electronic Unit, which manages pilot life support systems including cabin pressurisation and cockpit air-conditioning, while overseeing the complex fuel system. The company is developing a new Radio Altimeter for precise low-level altitude measurement, a VHF Omni-Range and Instrument Landing System for poor-weather approach guidance, and a Tactical Air Navigation System for military-grade directional and distance data. The LCA Mk2 will also feature the indigenous Uttam active electronically scanned array radar, a Unified Electronic Warfare Suite, an Infrared Search and Track system, and a triple-layer computing architecture comprising a Digital Flight Control Computer, Mission Management and Display Computer and an indigenous Auxiliary Computer that provides failover redundancy and computational offloading for tasks such as terrain mapping and electronic warfare threat classification.
The LCA Mk2 programme, sanctioned at approximately ten thousand crore rupees by the Cabinet Committee on Security in 2022, is designed to bridge the capability gap between the lighter Tejas Mk1A and India’s future fifth-generation Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft. With a maximum takeoff weight of seventeen-and-a-half tonnes, a payload capacity of six-and-a-half tonnes across eleven hardpoints, and internal fuel capacity exceeding three thousand four hundred kilograms, the aircraft is powered by the GE F414-INS6 engine producing ninety-eight kilonewtons of thrust. HAL CMD Ravi confirmed at the 2026 Farnborough Airshow that structural assembly of the first prototype is progressing and the aircraft will replace the Mirage 2000, Jaguar and MiG-29 fleets in the 2035 to 2040 timeframe. The indigenous fuel sensing and data acquisition technologies developed for this platform represent not merely component-level substitutions, but the creation of sovereign design capabilities that will feed forward into the AMCA programme, reducing lifecycle costs by up to thirty per cent through shared module architectures.

articles.title: Tejas-Based Trainer vs HLFT-42: Which Is Better for IAF’s 150-Jet Stage-III Trainer Requirement?
articles.text:
The Indian Air Force’s requirement for around 150 Stage-III (F) jet trainers has opened the possibility of one of the most consequential trainer aircraft competitions in India’s recent aerospace history. While the HAL HLFT-42 has been conceived specifically as an advanced jet trainer, a Tejas-derived twin-seat trainer could offer the Indian Air Force a different proposition: commonality with an aircraft already entering mass production, a shared logistics ecosystem and potentially a limited wartime combat role.
The choice could ultimately come down to whether the IAF prioritises a purpose-built trainer or a trainer built around an expanding indigenous fighter ecosystem.
Tejas-Based Trainer Offers a Major Commonality Advantage
The strongest argument for a Tejas-based Stage-III trainer is that the underlying platform is already being developed and produced for the IAF. Unlike a clean-sheet aircraft, a trainer derived from the Tejas family could potentially share significant portions of its avionics architecture, cockpit systems, ground-support equipment, maintenance practices, components and supply chain with India’s frontline light fighter fleet.
This commonality could become increasingly valuable if the IAF eventually operates more than 300 Tejas-family aircraft, including Tejas Mk-1A and future Tejas Mk-II variants. Instead of maintaining a completely separate advanced-training ecosystem, the IAF could potentially establish a pathway from basic training into a Tejas-family trainer and then directly into operational Tejas squadrons.
Such commonality could reduce the logistical burden while creating economies of scale for India’s aerospace industry.
HLFT-42 Has the Purpose-Built Trainer Advantage
The HLFT-42, meanwhile, has an important advantage: it is being designed specifically around the advanced jet-training mission. A clean-sheet trainer can be optimised for student-instructor visibility, cockpit ergonomics, handling characteristics, training sortie requirements, fatigue life, operating cost and emergency procedures.
This is particularly important because simply converting a fighter into a trainer does not automatically produce an ideal training aircraft. Adding a second cockpit changes the aircraft’s weight distribution, centre of gravity, aerodynamics and performance. A Tejas-derived trainer would therefore still require substantial engineering, flight testing and certification.
HLFT-42 would theoretically avoid some of these compromises because the training mission can be incorporated into the aircraft’s design from the beginning.
MUM-T Could Become a Major Differentiator
A Tejas-family trainer could also provide an opportunity to introduce pilots to manned-unmanned teaming (MUM-T) concepts. As the IAF moves towards networked combat operations involving fighters, unmanned combat aircraft and loyal-wingman systems, the advanced trainer could potentially become part of the same digital ecosystem.
A Tejas-derived trainer could eventually provide pilots with experience operating alongside unmanned platforms and managing networked assets. However, MUM-T capability would not automatically come from using a Tejas-derived airframe. Dedicated datalinks, mission software, autonomy systems and command-and-control architecture would still be required.
Industrial Benefits Could Be Significant
The 150-aircraft requirement is large enough to influence India’s aerospace manufacturing ecosystem. A Tejas-based trainer could potentially utilise an existing industrial base rather than establishing an entirely separate manufacturing and support chain.
For HAL and its private-sector suppliers, this could mean greater production volumes, improved economies of scale and a larger installed base of Indian-made aircraft systems. It could also strengthen India’s ability to support Tejas-family aircraft throughout their lifecycle. The HLFT-42, on the other hand, could create a new indigenous aircraft programme and provide HAL with experience in designing and manufacturing a purpose-built advanced trainer.
Which Aircraft Makes More Sense?
There is no automatic winner. If the IAF’s priority is pure Stage-III training performance, the HLFT-42 has the conceptual advantage of being designed specifically for the mission. If the priority is fleet commonality, industrial scale, logistics, potential wartime utility and integration with India’s expanding Tejas ecosystem, a Tejas-derived trainer could become a highly attractive alternative.
The most important question will therefore be whether HAL can demonstrate that a twin-seat Tejas-based trainer can meet the IAF’s Stage-III requirements without excessive development costs or compromises in training performance.
If it can, the 150-aircraft requirement could become much more than a Hawk replacement programme. It could become an opportunity to create a common Tejas-family training and combat ecosystem, potentially supporting hundreds of aircraft while simultaneously strengthening India’s indigenous aerospace manufacturing base.

articles.title: The Download: kids’ thoughts on AI, and female clones of male mice
articles.text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

How kids feel about AI, in their own words

—Jen Swetzoff and Keeley McNamara, the founding editors of Anyway, an independent print magazine for tweens and teens

When we set out to talk to kids about AI, we thought we knew what we’d hear. We expected stories about cheating, inspiring uses, and concerns like deepfakes or job destruction. But what we actually heard from kids aged 10 to 18 had tons of nuance.

Many were so deeply against AI or uninterested in making it part of their lives that they didn’t want to talk about it at all. Others worried about cheating, the environmental impact, or AI’s effect on creativity and critical thinking.

AI doesn’t yet seem to be something a lot of them are focused on—and they aren’t begging for it, the way they do for iPhones and Snapchat. But what surprised us most was how much young people could teach adults about AI. 

Meet the kids navigating an AI-filled future—and hear what they think of it.

Scientists just created female clones of male mice

Scientists have deliberately turned male mouse embryos into females for the first time. A team based in Japan used a CRISPR-based approach to remove the Y chromosome from male cells and create female clones of male mice. 

The feat could change the way scientists think about reproduction, says Takashi Ishiuchi, a reproductive biologist at the University of Yamanashi, who co-led the work. “There’s a fixed concept in our scientific field that we need both females and males for reproduction,” says Ishiuchi. “I think we could change this concept.”

He also hopes the technique could help rescue endangered species, particularly in cases where only a few individuals remain. Find out how it works—and what it could mean for the future of reproduction and conservation.

—Jessica Hamzelou

What’s behind this summer’s heat, and why 2027 could be worse

This summer has been a scorcher for much of the Northern Hemisphere. June and July marked the hottest two-month stretch in Europe since record-keeping began, the contiguous US endured its hottest month on record in July, and South Korea saw its highest-ever recorded temperature.  

Climate change makes heat waves more likely and more intense. But there’s another factor at play: El Niño, which is already ramping up and is expected to have a bigger effect on global temperatures next year.

Here’s what’s behind this summer’s extreme heat—and why 2027 could be even hotter.

—Casey Crownhart

This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

Inside the “censorship-industrial complex” idea shaping US policy

For years, the idea of a “censorship-industrial complex” that suppressed conservative and populist speech spread in right-wing circles online. But now, the theory has made its way into the Trump administration.

Over the past nine months, MIT Technology Review investigated its origins and traced its rise. 

In a virtual Roundtables session today, senior reporter Eileen Guo and executive editor Amy Nordrum will explore what they discovered, where the theory is going, and what it could mean for the future of democracy and the internet.

Register here to join the session at 19:00 GMT / 2:00 pm ET / 11:00 am PT.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

Vetted firms could use cyber tools against foreign criminal groups. (Reuters $)

ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini can all echo authoritarian propaganda. (WSJ $)
+ Turkey’s new cyber law has stoked fears of a digital police state. (FT $)

All streamers are opted in to train AI with their content by default. (404 Media)
+ Users can now opt out, but the announcement has sparked uproar. (BBC)
+ AI’s memories are privacy’s next frontier. (MIT Technology Review)

4 Trump has been sued over a service selling faster access to his social posts
The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation filed the suit. (NPR)
+ They call the service “corrupt” and “unconstitutional.” (Ars Technica)
+ And say it violates the right of equal access to official information. (Reuters $)

5 Police officers are using Flock cameras to stalk people
Three Georgia deputies are the latest officers accused of abuse. (NYT $)
+ But the surveillance devices still have some supporters. (Atlantic $)

6 AI reporters are now breaking big news
One just beat human journalists to a story about hacking at OpenAI. (Wired $)
+ The milestone has sparked debate about the future of journalism. (Gizmodo)

7 The web’s newest weapon against AI scrapers is a font
ShieldFont foils scrapers but keeps pages readable to people. (Ars Technica)

8 Live streaming has turned us all into Perez Hilton
It’s made us both the celebrity and the paparazzi. (New Yorker $)

It pushes the origin of mammalian live birth back 95 million years. (New Scientist $)

New research disputes claims that science is getting less disruptive. (Economist $)

Quote of the day

“Trump is trying to enrich himself by privatizing government information that he has no right to sell. We won’t let it stand.” 

—Ben Muessig, editor-in-chief of The Intercept, explains why his media organization is suing President Trump over his fast-access service to Truth Social posts.

One More Thing


Puerto Rico’s power struggles

Carmen Suárez Vázquez lives just minutes from Puerto Rico’s only coal-fired power plant. Black dust coats her windowpanes and the leaves of the blooming vines around her home. She doesn’t know exactly how the coal pollution got inside, but she is certain it ended up in her youngest son, Edgardo, who died of a rare form of cancer.

The plant was supposed to close in 2027. Instead, it will stay open for at least another seven years, while Puerto Rico rolls back clean-energy targets and moves ahead with new gas plants.

Meanwhile, residents are still dealing with frequent blackouts and high electricity prices. And an unelected fiscal control board has veto power over all spending by the island’s elected government, leaving Puerto Ricans with little say over their energy future.

Here’s why Puerto Rico can’t seem to escape its energy crisis.
